title: Type conversions: intent, information loss, and range checks
goal: Compare conversion before division with conversion after the fraction is lost.

prerequisites.text: You understand int, double and integer division.

sections.title: From the task to an operation
paragraphs: If both operands are integers, 5/2 gives 2. Storing that result in double gives 2.0: the fraction has already been lost. static_cast<double>(count) explicitly obtains a double value from count before division. With a double operand, division is performed in a floating-point type.

An explicit conversion states intent but does not make every value safe. double→int discards the fraction toward zero, and the value must be within range. Brace initialization rejects many narrowing conversions to detect loss early. Here 5 and 2 are small and exactly representable.

sections.title: Compare conversion before division with conversion after the fraction is lost.
trace: Conversion after division cannot recover the fraction.
A floating-point operand exists before division.

sections.title: Change one condition and check the prediction
When the result differs
paragraphs: static_cast<double>(count/people) still converts a completed integer quotient and gives 2.

sections.title: Now solve your own task
paragraphs: Divide 9 items between two people. Show the integer quotient and floating-point share; convert an operand before the operation.
Practice contains a separate starter. Predict the result before changing your program. Returning to the example does not replace your source.

Divide 9 items between two people. Show the integer quotient and floating-point share; convert an operand before the operation.
selfcheck.feedback: Compare the output with the readable reference case below. Explain each change using the objects or operations in this topic. 9/2 gives 4, while static_cast<double>(items)/people gives 4.5. static_cast<double>(items/people) gives 4 because conversion happens after integer division.
